units.title: Thinking Like Scientists and Engineers
units.big_idea: Scientists ask questions and investigate; engineers define problems and design solutions.

units.title: Properties of Materials
units.big_idea: Materials have properties we can observe and test, and we choose materials whose properties fit the job.

units.title: Building Blocks and Changing Matter
units.big_idea: Objects can be taken apart and rebuilt into new things, and heating or cooling changes some materials for good.

units.title: What Plants Need
units.big_idea: Plants need water and light to grow, and fair tests show what they need.

units.title: Seeds, Pollinators, and Plant Partners
units.big_idea: Plants depend on animals to move pollen and spread seeds.

units.title: Habitats and Biodiversity
units.big_idea: Different habitats hold different kinds and numbers of living things.

units.title: Earth's Changes, Fast and Slow
units.big_idea: Some Earth events happen in minutes and others take thousands of years.

units.title: Wind, Water, and Protecting the Land
units.big_idea: Wind and water reshape land, and people design solutions to slow erosion.

units.title: Maps of Land and Water
units.big_idea: Models and maps show the shapes of land and water, and Earth's water can be solid or liquid.

units.title: Engineering Showcase
units.big_idea: Engineers use what they know about materials and Earth to design, test, and improve solutions.

objectives: Make observations using senses and tools

days.title: Science notebook
days.work: Set up a science notebook with a cover, table of contents, and a page on 'What scientists do.' Draw and label a magnifying glass.

days.title: Nature observation
days.work: Collect 5 natural objects outside and observe each with a magnifier; record color, shape, texture, and size in a chart.

days.title: Asking questions
days.work: Sort questions about the objects into 'can test' and 'can't test' and write 3 testable questions (Which rock is heaviest?).

days.title: Measure and compare
days.work: Use a ruler and kitchen scale to measure the objects and order them by size and weight.

days.title: Review
days.work: Share notebook observations aloud and explain the difference between an observation and an opinion.

weeks.assessment: Notebook observation chart and 3 testable questions.

days.title: What engineers do
days.work: Look at everyday tools (can opener, clothespin, zipper) and discuss what problem each solves; record 3 in your notebook.

days.title: Define the problem
days.work: Problem: pencils keep rolling off the table. Ask questions and list what a solution must do.

days.title: Sketch
days.work: Sketch two designs for a pencil holder from paper and tape and label how the shape keeps pencils from rolling.

days.title: Build & test
days.work: Build the best design and test it with 5 pencils; record results and one improvement.

days.title: Review
days.work: Explain the design steps (ask, imagine, plan, create, improve) using your pencil holder as the example.

weeks.assessment: Labeled design sketch and test results.

objectives: Describe materials by color, texture, hardness, flexibility
materials: wood, metal, plastic, fabric, paper, rubber objects

days.title: Material hunt
days.work: Find 15 household objects and identify what material each is made of (wood, metal, plastic, glass, fabric, paper, rubber).

days.title: Properties
days.work: Describe each material's properties (hard/soft, rough/smooth, bendy/stiff, shiny/dull) in a table.

days.title: Sort and classify
days.work: Sort the objects two different ways (by material, then by a property) and explain the rule for each sort.

days.title: Mystery bag
days.work: Identify objects in a bag by touch alone and name their texture and hardness.

days.title: Review
days.work: Classify 10 new objects by material and properties and justify one classification aloud.

weeks.assessment: Material/property classification table.

objectives: Plan and conduct a fair test
Decide which material is best for a purpose
materials: paper towel, napkin, sponge, cloth, plastic wrap, foil

days.title: Plan a test
days.work: Plan a fair test of which material absorbs water best: same amount of water, same size pieces. Write predictions.

days.title: Absorbency test
days.work: Drop 10 drops (or spoonfuls) of water on each material and observe what happens; record in a data table.

days.title: Waterproof test
days.work: Test which materials keep a paper doll dry under drips (foil, plastic wrap, cloth, paper).

days.title: Analyze
days.work: Make a bar graph of results and decide the best material for a raincoat and for cleaning a spill.

days.title: Review
days.work: Write a claim and evidence sentence: 'The best material for a raincoat is ___ because ___.'

weeks.assessment: Data table, bar graph, and claim-evidence sentence.

objectives: Test strength and flexibility of materials
materials: strips of paper, foil, fabric, plastic bag

days.title: Strength test
days.work: Hang a paper cup from strips of different materials and add pennies until each breaks; record the number.

days.title: Flexibility test
days.work: Bend strips of cardboard, plastic, wood craft sticks, and foil and rank them from most to least flexible.

days.title: Stretch test
days.work: Measure how far rubber bands and fabric strips stretch with a ruler.

days.title: Best for the job
days.work: Use data to pick the best material for a bag handle, a bridge deck, and a hair tie; explain with numbers.

days.title: Review
days.work: Present test results in a chart and answer 'Why do engineers test materials?'

weeks.assessment: Strength data chart and material-choice explanations.

objectives: Test which materials keep things cold
Use data to identify strengths and weaknesses

days.title: Melting predictions
days.work: Predict which wrapper (foil, cloth, newspaper, bubble wrap, none) will keep an ice cube from melting longest.

days.title: Ice cube test
days.work: Wrap identical ice cubes and check every 15 minutes; record observations and time to melt.

days.title: Design an ice keeper
days.work: Design and build an 'ice cube keeper' from two materials and sketch it.

days.title: Compare designs
days.work: Test your keeper vs. the best single material; record data and compare strengths and weaknesses.

days.title: Review
days.work: Write a notebook conclusion about which materials make good insulators and why.

weeks.assessment: Ice-keeper design test with data comparison.

weeks.topic: Materials unit project: build a better umbrella
objectives: Apply property data to a design challenge
materials: craft sticks, straws, foil, plastic bag, fabric, tape

days.title: Define the problem
days.work: Design a mini umbrella to keep a small toy dry; list criteria (waterproof, sturdy, light).

days.title: Choose materials
days.work: Use data from earlier tests to choose materials and sketch the design with labels.

days.title: Build
days.work: Build the umbrella and test it under a spray bottle for 30 seconds.

days.title: Improve
days.work: Improve one part and retest; record how the change affected results.

days.title: Unit 2 check
days.work: Present the umbrella and explain material choices; complete a short quiz on classifying materials by properties.

weeks.assessment: Umbrella design presentation and properties quiz.

objectives: Disassemble and rebuild into a new object

days.title: Build a house
days.work: Build a small house from 20 blocks and draw it; count pieces of each type.

days.title: Take apart
days.work: Take the house apart and build a new object (car or bridge) using the same 20 pieces; draw it.

days.title: Same pieces, new shape
days.work: Compare the two drawings and explain how the same pieces made different objects.

days.title: Real world
days.work: Look at pictures of a wooden fence turned into a table or bricks reused in a building; discuss.

days.title: Review
days.work: Write an evidence-based account: 'I know an object made of pieces can become a new object because…'

weeks.assessment: Written evidence account with drawings.

weeks.topic: Reversible changes with heating and cooling
objectives: Observe changes when materials are heated or cooled
Identify changes that can be reversed

days.title: Freeze and melt
days.work: Freeze water in ice trays and then melt the cubes; record that water becomes ice and back again.

days.title: Chocolate change
days.work: Melt chocolate chips in a bag in warm water, then cool them in the fridge; observe the shape change and reversal.

days.title: Crayon remake
days.work: With an adult, melt broken crayon pieces in a muffin tin in the oven at low heat and cool them into new crayons.

days.title: Before and after
days.work: Make a before/heated/cooled chart for the three investigations.

days.title: Review
days.work: Explain which changes were reversible and give evidence from the chart.

weeks.assessment: Before/after chart and reversible-change explanation.

objectives: Observe changes that cannot be reversed

days.title: Cooking an egg
days.work: Observe a raw egg, then cook it with an adult; discuss whether it can become raw again.

days.title: Toast
days.work: Toast a slice of bread and compare to untoasted bread; try to 'untoast' it (cooling) and record.

days.title: Pancakes
days.work: Make pancakes and describe how liquid batter becomes solid when heated.

days.title: Sort changes
days.work: Sort 12 picture cards (melting snow, baking a cake, freezing juice, burning wood) into reversible/irreversible.

days.title: Review
days.work: Write an argument: 'Some changes caused by heating can be reversed and some cannot,' with two pieces of evidence each.

weeks.assessment: Change-sort and written argument with evidence.

objectives: Apply understanding of pieces and changes to a project
Design a new object from old pieces

days.title: Plan
days.work: Collect clean recyclables and plan a new object (toy, organizer) to build from them; sketch it.

days.title: Build
days.work: Build the object with glue and tape, counting how many of each piece you used, and label its parts.

days.title: Rebuild
days.work: Disassemble and rebuild into a second, different object; photograph or draw both.

days.title: Ice pop test
days.work: Freeze juice pops and let one melt and refreeze; discuss if it is the same as before.

days.title: Unit 3 check
days.work: Quiz on pieces/new objects and reversible/irreversible changes; present the recycled builds.

weeks.assessment: Recycled-object presentation and unit quiz.

weeks.topic: Parts of plants and plant needs
objectives: Identify plant parts and their jobs
Ask questions about what plants need

days.title: Plant parts
days.work: Dig up a weed and identify roots, stem, leaves, and flowers; draw and label it.

days.title: Celery straw
days.work: Put a celery stalk in colored water and observe how water travels up the stem over a day.

days.title: Seed in a bag
days.work: Plant bean seeds in wet paper towels in a zip bag on a window to watch roots grow.

days.title: What do plants need?
days.work: List what you think plants need and write questions to test (Do plants need light? Water?).

days.title: Review
days.work: Record day-by-day observations of celery and bean bag; explain the stem's job.

weeks.assessment: Labeled plant drawing and observation log.

weeks.topic: Fair test: Do plants need light?
objectives: Plan and conduct a fair test about light
materials: 4 bean plants or seedlings in cups

days.title: Plan the light test
days.work: Plan a fair test: 2 plants in sunlight, 2 in a dark closet, same water and soil. Write predictions.

days.title: Set up
days.work: Set up the four plants, label each cup (light/dark), and measure and record each plant's starting height in centimeters.

days.title: Observe
days.work: Measure each plant's height and note its leaf color and stem shape; record the numbers in the data table.

days.title: Midweek check
days.work: Draw both groups and compare color (green vs. yellow) and stem shape.

days.title: Review
days.work: Explain why only light was changed and what we keep the same in a fair test.

weeks.assessment: Investigation plan and data table.

weeks.topic: Fair test: Do plants need water?
objectives: Plan and conduct a fair test about water

days.title: Plan the water test
days.work: Set up 2 watered plants and 2 unwatered plants in the same light; predict results.

days.title: Measure light test
days.work: Measure the light-test plants and graph height over time.

days.title: Observe water test
days.work: Observe and record wilting, color, and height of the water-test plants.

days.title: Graph
days.work: Make bar graphs comparing plants with and without light and water.

days.title: Review
days.work: Share the two graphs with a family member and explain which plants look healthiest and what surprised you.

weeks.assessment: Two bar graphs of plant growth.

days.title: Final measurements
days.work: Take final measurements of all plants and complete the data tables.

days.title: Conclusion
days.work: Write a conclusion: 'Plants need ___ and ___ to grow. My evidence is…'

days.title: Rescue
days.work: Move the closet and unwatered plants to light and water; predict whether they recover.

days.title: Poster
days.work: Make a poster of the investigation (question, prediction, test, results, conclusion).

days.title: Unit 4 check
days.work: Present the poster and complete a quiz on plant needs and fair tests.

weeks.assessment: Investigation poster and unit quiz.

materials: assorted seeds (maple, dandelion, burrs, acorns, fruit seeds)

days.title: Seed collection
days.work: Collect seeds outside or from fruits and sort them by how you think they travel (wind, water, animals, fur).

days.title: Sock walk
days.work: Walk through a grassy area wearing an old sock over a shoe; observe and count seeds that stick.

days.title: Wind test
days.work: Use a fan to test which seeds travel farthest; measure distances.

days.title: Animals eat fruit
days.work: Read about birds eating berries and dropping seeds; draw a seed's journey from fruit to new plant.

days.title: Review
days.work: Match 8 seeds to their dispersal method with reasons.

weeks.assessment: Seed dispersal matching and journey drawing.

objectives: Develop a model that mimics an animal dispersing seeds

days.title: Design challenge
days.work: Design a model 'animal' that picks up and carries seeds like fur does; sketch two ideas.

days.title: Build
days.work: Build the model 'animal' from a sock, fabric scraps, Velcro, or pipe-cleaner 'fur,' following your sketch.

days.title: Test
days.work: Drag the model through a tray of seeds or rice and count seeds picked up and dropped.

days.title: Improve
days.work: Change the model's shape or material and retest; record changes.

days.title: Review
days.work: Explain how the model is like a real animal and how its shape helps it work.

weeks.assessment: Model test data and explanation.

days.title: Flower parts
days.work: Dissect a flower (or use a diagram) to find petals and pollen; draw and label.

days.title: Pollinator observation
days.work: Watch flowers outside for 15 minutes and tally bees, butterflies, and birds.

days.title: Cheese puff model
days.work: Use fingers dusted with cheese puff powder to 'visit' paper flowers; observe how 'pollen' moves.

days.title: Pollinator research
days.work: Read about bees, hummingbirds, and bats as pollinators; record one fact each.

days.title: Review
days.work: Explain why plants need pollinators and pollinators need plants.

weeks.assessment: Pollination model and explanation.

objectives: Develop a model that mimics a pollinator

days.title: Plan
days.work: Design a 'hand pollinator' tool that moves colored powder from flower to flower; sketch.

days.title: Build
days.work: Build the hand pollinator from pipe cleaners, cotton balls, and craft sticks, shaping the tip to reach into a paper flower.

days.title: Test
days.work: Test how well it picks up and drops powder on paper flowers; record results.

days.title: Compare
days.work: Compare two designs and decide which works better and why.

days.title: Unit 5 check
days.work: Present the model and take a quiz on seed dispersal and pollination.

weeks.assessment: Pollinator model presentation and unit quiz.

weeks.topic: What is a habitat? Surveying living things nearby
objectives: Observe and count kinds of living things in a local area
Compare two local areas with data
materials: field guide or iNaturalist Seek app (optional)

days.title: Habitat needs
days.work: Learn that a habitat provides food, water, shelter, and space; walk around the block and list 4 small habitats (tree, lawn, garden bed, puddle) with one animal that lives in each.

days.title: Hoop survey 1
days.work: Lay a hoop on a lawn or garden bed, search it for 15 minutes with a magnifier, and tally every different kind of plant and animal (ants, clover, beetles, grass) in a survey sheet.

days.title: Hoop survey 2
days.work: Repeat the same 15-minute hoop survey in a very different spot (sidewalk crack, gravel, or under a tree) and tally kinds of living things the same way.

days.title: Graph the data
days.work: Make a bar graph comparing the number of different kinds of living things found in each spot, and circle any organism found in both places.

days.title: Review
days.work: Write a claim with evidence: 'The ___ spot had more kinds of living things because it had more ___ (water, shade, plants),' and share it aloud.

weeks.assessment: Hoop-survey data, bar graph, and claim-evidence sentence.

weeks.topic: Comparing land habitats: forest, desert, grassland
objectives: Compare diversity in three land habitats
Gather information from books and videos
materials: library habitat books (e.g., A Walk in the Desert, Rebecca L. Johnson)

days.title: Forest
days.work: Read a library book or National Geographic Kids article about a redwood forest and list 8 plants and animals that live there, noting where each finds shelter.

days.title: Desert
days.work: Read about California's Mojave Desert and list the living things (Joshua tree, tortoise, roadrunner, cactus); discuss how each survives with little water.

days.title: Grassland
days.work: Watch a short video about California grasslands or the prairie and list the plants and animals; tally how many kinds each source names.

days.title: Compare chart
days.work: Make a three-column chart and a bar graph of how many kinds of living things each habitat has; describe the pattern you see.

days.title: Review
days.work: Answer in 3–4 sentences: 'Which habitat has the most diversity, and why?' using evidence from the chart (more water and plants support more animals).

weeks.assessment: Habitat comparison chart and written answer with evidence.

weeks.topic: Comparing water habitats: kelp forest, pond, tide pool
objectives: Compare diversity in ocean and freshwater habitats
materials: Monterey Bay Aquarium kelp cam or ocean video

days.title: Kelp forest
days.work: Watch the Monterey Bay Aquarium kelp forest live cam or a kelp video for 10 minutes and list every kind of fish, plant, and animal you see.

days.title: Pond sample
days.work: Scoop pond or puddle water into a clear jar with an adult, let it settle, and look for tiny swimming organisms with a magnifier; draw 3 you find (or use pond-life photos).

days.title: Tide pool
days.work: Read about California tide pools and sketch a tide pool with sea stars, anemones, crabs, and snails, labeling where each lives (rock, water, crack).

days.title: Land vs. water
days.work: Add the three water habitats to last week's chart and compare totals with the land habitats; note which habitat had the most kinds overall.

days.title: Review
days.work: Tell a family member which habitat surprised you most and give two facts as evidence; answer 2 questions they ask.

weeks.assessment: Updated habitat chart and oral explanation with evidence.

objectives: Build a model of a habitat
Show the diversity of living things in it
materials: construction paper, clay, twigs, sand, cotton

days.title: Choose and research
days.work: Choose one habitat (redwood forest, Mojave Desert, kelp forest, tide pool, or pond) and use 2 sources to list 6 living things and what each needs.

days.title: Build the background
days.work: Paint or line a shoebox to show the habitat's land, water, and sky, and add plants made from paper, twigs, or clay.

days.title: Add animals and labels
days.work: Model at least 4 animals in clay or paper and add index-card labels telling what each eats and where it shelters.

days.title: Present
days.work: Present the diorama, naming how many kinds of living things it shows, and compare it with one habitat from the chart (more or less diversity and why).

days.title: Unit 6 check
days.work: Quiz: match 8 organisms to habitats and explain which of two pictured habitats has more diversity.

weeks.assessment: Diorama presentation (rubric) and unit quiz.

weeks.topic: Fast Earth changes: volcanoes, earthquakes, landslides
objectives: Describe Earth events that happen quickly

days.title: Mount St. Helens
days.work: Compare before-and-after photos of Mount St. Helens (1980) and read a short passage about the eruption; record how much the mountain changed in one day.

days.title: Model volcano
days.work: Build a clay volcano around a cup, erupt it with baking soda and vinegar, and draw how the 'lava' changed the land around it.

days.title: Earthquake shake table
days.work: Build a block tower on a tray resting on marbles, shake the tray, and record what happens; read about a California earthquake and how quickly it changed roads.

days.title: Landslide
days.work: Pack damp soil on a tilted tray, pour water at the top, and time how fast the soil slides; compare to photos of a California coastal landslide.

days.title: Review
days.work: Fill a 3-row chart (event, how long it took, evidence and source) for the volcano, earthquake, and landslide.

weeks.assessment: Fast-change evidence chart citing at least two sources.

weeks.topic: Slow Earth changes: weathering and erosion
objectives: Describe Earth changes that happen slowly
materials: sugar cubes and jar with lid

days.title: Shake and break
days.work: Shake 5 sugar cubes in a jar for 2 minutes, then 2 more, and compare the corners each time to model how rocks bumping in rivers are worn down.

days.title: Rock rubbing
days.work: Rub two rough rocks together over black paper for 2 minutes and look at the dust with a magnifier; discuss how long it would take to wear a rock away.

days.title: Grand Canyon
days.work: Read about how the Colorado River carved the Grand Canyon over millions of years and look at the rock layers in photos; write 2 facts.

days.title: Ice cracks rock
days.work: Fill a small plastic container to the top with water, cap it, freeze overnight, and observe how the ice bulged or cracked the container.

days.title: Review
days.work: Write 3 sentences explaining why weathering and erosion change land so slowly, using evidence from the sugar cube and ice tests.

weeks.assessment: Weathering observations and written explanation.

weeks.topic: Comparing fast and slow changes on a timeline
objectives: Sort Earth events by how long they take
Build a timeline of time scales
Compare a fast and a slow change in writing

days.title: Sort events
days.work: Sort 12 picture cards (flood, eruption, canyon, earthquake, sand dune, landslide, glacier valley) into fast and slow and justify 3 choices aloud.

days.title: Time scale strip
days.work: Make a long paper timeline with marks for seconds, hours, days, years, and millions of years, and place each event card where it belongs.

days.title: Yosemite Valley
days.work: Read two short sources about how glaciers carved Yosemite Valley slowly and how a rockfall can happen in seconds; list evidence from each.

days.title: Compare in writing
days.work: Write a paragraph comparing one fast change and one slow change: what happened, how long it took, and how you know.

days.title: Review
days.work: Read the paragraph aloud and answer a family member's questions; check that each claim names a source.

weeks.assessment: Time-scale strip and comparison paragraph.

weeks.topic: Earth changes model and unit check
objectives: Compare a model to the real world
Show understanding of fast and slow changes
materials: sand or soil in a long pan
watering can or cup with pinhole

days.title: Notebook review
days.work: Review notebook entries on fast and slow changes and highlight the strongest piece of evidence for each.

days.title: Sand canyon model
days.work: Tilt a pan of damp sand and let water trickle from a pinhole cup for 10 minutes; photograph or sketch the 'canyon' every 2 minutes.

days.title: Model vs. real
days.work: Compare the sand canyon to Grand Canyon photos; list 2 ways the model is like the real canyon and 1 way it is different (time).

days.title: Poster
days.work: Make a 'Fast vs. Slow' poster with drawings, time labels, and one piece of evidence from a source for each event.

days.title: Unit 7 check
days.work: Quiz: classify 8 events as fast or slow and explain one using evidence; present the poster.

weeks.assessment: Poster and unit quiz.

weeks.topic: How wind and water change land
objectives: Observe how wind and water move soil and sand

days.title: Water erosion
days.work: Build a sand hill in a tray, sprinkle it with a watering can for 1 minute, and draw where sand was removed and where it was deposited.

days.title: Wind erosion
days.work: Make a flat sand pile on newspaper, blow through a straw from 10 cm away for 30 seconds, and measure how far sand traveled.

days.title: Erosion walk
days.work: Walk the neighborhood or a park to photograph or sketch erosion (gullies, exposed tree roots, washed-out paths) and note whether water or wind caused it.

days.title: Coastal erosion
days.work: Read about California cliff erosion (e.g., Pacifica) and look at photos of homes near eroding cliffs; discuss why it is a problem for people.

days.title: Review
days.work: Draw before-and-after pictures of the water and wind models and label erosion and deposit areas.

weeks.assessment: Before/after erosion drawings with labels.

objectives: Compare results in a data table
materials: two trays of soil (one planted with grass seed two weeks earlier or covered with moss)

days.title: Real solutions
days.work: Look at photos of retaining walls, rows of trees as windbreaks, levees, and sand fences, and write what problem each solves.

days.title: Plants vs. bare soil
days.work: Pour 2 cups of water down a tray of bare soil and a tray with grass growing; collect and compare the muddy runoff in cups.

days.title: Barriers
days.work: Build a craft-stick wall and a pebble wall on a sand hill and test each with the same amount of water; measure how much sand moves.

days.title: Data table
days.work: Record results of all four tests (bare, grass, sticks, pebbles) in a table and rank them from least to most sand lost.

days.title: Review
days.work: Write which solution worked best and one weakness of it, using the data as evidence.

weeks.assessment: Solution test data table and written conclusion.

weeks.topic: Design challenge: protect the house on the hill
objectives: Design, build, and test two solutions
materials: craft sticks, foil, cloth, pebbles, clay

days.title: Define the problem
days.work: A toy house sits on a sand hill near a 'river'; list the criteria (house stays put after 2 cups of water) and constraints (only 10 craft sticks, pebbles, clay).

days.title: Sketch two designs
days.work: Sketch two different solutions (e.g., a wall vs. a channel that moves water away) and label how each shape protects the house.

days.title: Build & test design 1
days.work: Build design 1, pour 2 cups of water, and measure how far the house moved and how much sand washed away.

days.title: Build & test design 2
days.work: Rebuild the hill, build design 2, and test it the same way; record results in the same table.

days.title: Review
days.work: Compare the two designs in a T-chart of strengths and weaknesses and decide which to improve.

weeks.assessment: Design sketches and comparison T-chart with data.

objectives: Improve a design using test data

days.title: Improve
days.work: Change one feature of the better design (taller wall, added 'plants') and retest; record whether results improved.

days.title: Poster
days.work: Make a poster showing the problem, both designs, test data, and the improved design.

days.title: Present
days.work: Present the poster to family, explaining why the improved design worked better, and answer 2 questions.

days.title: Real world
days.work: Read about sand dunes and dune grass protecting California beaches and compare them to your designs.

days.title: Unit 8 check
days.work: Quiz: identify erosion in 4 photos and choose the best solution for 3 situations with a reason.

weeks.assessment: Design poster presentation and unit quiz.

objectives: Name and describe landforms and bodies of water
Build a model of land and water

days.title: Landforms
days.work: Sort photos of mountains, hills, valleys, plains, islands, and peninsulas and write a one-line definition for each.

days.title: Bodies of water
days.work: Learn ocean, lake, river, pond, stream, and bay, and find a California example of each on a map (Pacific Ocean, Lake Tahoe, Sacramento River, San Francisco Bay).

days.title: Build a model
days.work: Build a clay landscape in a pan with a mountain, valley, island, and peninsula, then add water to form a lake, river, and ocean.

days.title: Label
days.work: Label each feature with toothpick flags and photograph the model from above and from the side.

days.title: Review
days.work: Explain the model to a family member, pointing to each landform and body of water and telling how they differ.

weeks.assessment: Labeled landform model and oral explanation.

objectives: Draw a map of land and water from a model
Use a map key and compass rose

days.title: California map
days.work: Study a physical map of California and find the Sierra Nevada, Central Valley, Sacramento River, Lake Tahoe, and Pacific coast; mark them on a blank outline.

days.title: Map key
days.work: Create a map key with colors and symbols for mountains, valleys, rivers, lakes, and ocean.

days.title: Map the model
days.work: Use the bird's-eye photo of last week's model to draw a map with the key and a compass rose.

days.title: Neighborhood map
days.work: Draw a map of your neighborhood or a nearby park showing hills, creeks, ponds, or the coast, with a key.

days.title: Review
days.work: Compare the model and the map: what does the map show well and what does the model show well (height)?

weeks.assessment: Model map and California map with key.

weeks.topic: Where water is found: solid and liquid
objectives: Identify where water is found on Earth
Explain that water can be solid or liquid

days.title: Water planet
days.work: Spin a globe and stop it with a finger 20 times, tallying land vs. water; color oceans, ice caps, and large lakes on a world map.

days.title: Solid and liquid
days.work: Observe ice melting in a cup, then list where water is solid on Earth (glaciers, snow, ice caps) and where it is liquid (oceans, rivers, lakes).

days.title: Sierra snowpack
days.work: Read about the Sierra Nevada snowpack melting in spring and filling rivers and reservoirs; draw the path of water from snow to faucet.

days.title: Fresh vs. salt
days.work: Taste-test (with an adult) a cup of fresh water and a cup of salty water; sort water bodies into fresh and salt on a chart.

days.title: Unit 9 check
days.work: Quiz: label landforms and water on a map, and identify where water is solid or liquid on Earth.

weeks.assessment: Water-sources chart and unit quiz.

objectives: Build, test, and improve a bridge
materials: two stacks of books 20 cm apart

days.title: Define the problem
days.work: Problem: build a bridge across a 20-cm 'river' between two book stacks that holds a cup of pennies; list criteria and limits (10 straws, 1 sheet of paper, 50 cm of tape).

days.title: Sketch and choose
days.work: Sketch two bridge designs (flat, folded accordion, arch) and choose materials using your strength-test data from Unit 2.

days.title: Build
days.work: Build the chosen bridge and check that it spans the gap without touching the 'water.'

days.title: Test
days.work: Hang a cup from the bridge and add pennies one at a time, recording the count when it sags or falls.

days.title: Improve
days.work: Change one part (fold the paper, add a straw truss) and retest; record the new penny count.

weeks.assessment: Bridge design sketches and load-test data.

days.title: Compare bridges
days.work: Make a T-chart comparing the first and improved bridges' strengths and weaknesses and explain which shape worked best.

days.title: Choose investigations
days.work: Review the science notebook and choose 3 favorite investigations (e.g., plant needs, ice keeper, erosion design) to display.

days.title: Build the display
days.work: Make a science fair board with the question, test, data, and conclusion for each chosen investigation.

days.title: Present
days.work: Present the science fair board to family or friends, demonstrating one investigation live.

days.title: Year-end check
days.work: Take a year-end review quiz covering materials, heating and cooling, plant needs, pollination, habitats, and Earth changes.

weeks.assessment: Science fair presentation and year-end quiz.

courses.subject: HSS
courses.title: People Who Make a Difference
courses.description: Grade 2 History–Social Science following the California 'People Who Make a Difference' course. Students trace their own family history with photographs, artifacts, and interviews; build map skills from a letter-number grid of their neighborhood to a map of North America; learn how laws are made, carried out, and judged and how nations cooperate; follow food from farm to table as producers and consumers; and study the lives of people who made a difference, from Abraham Lincoln and George Washington Carver to Marie Curie, Jackie Robinson, Cesar Chavez, and Sally Ride. Every unit uses primary sources such as photographs, letters, maps, and documents from the Library of Congress, National Archives, and Calisphere.
courses.framework: California History–Social Science Content Standards (Grade 2: People Who Make a Difference); 2016 California History–Social Science Framework

standards.2.1: Differentiate between things that happened long ago and things that happened yesterday.
standards.2.1.1: Trace the history of a family through primary and secondary sources, including artifacts, photographs, interviews, and documents.
standards.2.1.2: Compare and contrast daily lives with those of parents, grandparents, and/or guardians.
standards.2.1.3: Place important events in their lives in the order in which they occurred (e.g., on a time line or storyboard).
standards.2.2: Demonstrate map skills by describing the absolute and relative locations of people, places, and environments.
standards.2.2.1: Locate on a simple letter-number grid system the specific locations and geographic features in their neighborhood or community.
standards.2.2.2: Label from memory a simple map of North America (countries, oceans, Great Lakes, major rivers, mountain ranges) and identify map elements: title, legend, directional indicator, scale, and date.
standards.2.2.3: Locate on a map where their ancestors live(d), telling when the family moved to the local community and how and why they made the trip.
standards.2.2.4: Compare and contrast basic land use in urban, suburban, and rural environments in California.
standards.2.3: Explain governmental institutions and practices in the United States and other countries.
standards.2.3.1: Explain how the United States and other countries make laws, carry out laws, determine whether laws have been violated, and punish wrongdoers.
standards.2.3.2: Describe the ways in which groups and nations interact to try to resolve problems in such areas as trade, cultural contacts, treaties, diplomacy, and military force.
standards.2.4: Understand basic economic concepts and their individual roles in the economy, and demonstrate basic economic reasoning skills.
standards.2.4.1: Describe food production and consumption long ago and today, including the roles of farmers, processors, distributors, weather, and land and water resources.
standards.2.4.2: Understand the role and interdependence of buyers (consumers) and sellers (producers) of goods and services.
standards.2.4.3: Understand how limits on resources affect production and consumption (what to produce and what to consume).
standards.2.5: Understand the importance of individual action and character and explain how heroes from long ago and the recent past have made a difference in others' lives (e.g., Abraham Lincoln, Louis Pasteur, Sitting Bull, George Washington Carver, Marie Curie, Albert Einstein, Golda Meir, Jackie Robinson, Sally Ride).

units.title: My Family's Story: Long Ago and Today
units.big_idea: Families have histories we can uncover with photos, artifacts, documents, and interviews, and daily life has changed over time.

units.title: Maps and Where We Live
units.big_idea: Maps help us describe where people and places are, from our neighborhood to North America.

units.title: Rules, Laws, and Government
units.big_idea: Governments make laws, carry them out, and decide when they have been broken, to keep people safe and treat them fairly.

units.title: Getting Along: How Groups and Nations Solve Problems
units.big_idea: Groups and nations solve problems through trade, sharing cultures, agreements, and talking things out.

units.title: Producers, Consumers, and Our Food
units.big_idea: Many people and resources work together to bring food from farms to our tables, and limited resources mean making choices.

units.title: People Who Make a Difference
units.big_idea: Ordinary people with courage, curiosity, and hard work have changed the lives of others.

units.title: Celebrating Our Stories
units.big_idea: Our families, communities, and heroes are all part of history.

weeks.topic: What is history? Long ago and yesterday
objectives: Distinguish long ago, yesterday, today, and tomorrow
Sort objects from past and present

days.title: Yesterday, today, tomorrow
days.work: Use a calendar to label yesterday, today, and tomorrow and write one thing you did yesterday; discuss what 'long ago' means (before you were born).

days.title: Then and now objects
days.work: Compare pairs of objects (rotary phone vs. smartphone, washboard vs. washing machine photo) and sort 10 picture cards into 'long ago' and 'today.'

days.title: Primary sources
days.work: Look at a Library of Congress photo of children around 1910 and ask: Who? What? When? What clues tell us it is long ago? Record 3 clues.

days.title: History detectives
days.work: Learn the difference between a primary source (made at the time) and a secondary source (made later); sort 6 items (a diary, a textbook, a photo, a birth certificate).

days.title: Review
days.work: Draw a 'long ago' and a 'today' picture of a child's day and label 3 differences.

weeks.assessment: Then/now sort and labeled comparison drawing.

objectives: Place events of my life in order
Use words like first, then, before, after

days.title: Order events
days.work: Put 6 picture cards of a morning routine in order, then talk through the events of your own life using before and after.

days.title: Gather facts
days.work: Ask a parent for your birth date and 6 important events (first steps, first tooth, starting school, a move, a sibling's birth) with years.

days.title: Build the timeline
days.work: Make a timeline on adding-machine tape with one mark per year from birth to now and place each event with a drawing or photo.

days.title: Storyboard
days.work: Make a 4-box storyboard of one year of your life and tell it aloud in order.

days.title: Review
days.work: Present the timeline and answer questions using 'first, next, before, after, last.'

weeks.assessment: Personal timeline with events in correct order.

objectives: Use artifacts and documents to learn family history
materials: family artifacts (old photos, letters, recipe cards, tools)

days.title: Artifact museum
days.work: Collect 3–5 family artifacts and set up a home 'museum'; write a label for each telling what it is and who used it.

days.title: Ask the artifact
days.work: Use the questions 'What is it? Who used it? When? Why was it important?' to study one artifact and draw it.

days.title: Documents
days.work: Look at a family document (birth certificate copy, old letter, recipe card, or report card) and record 3 facts it tells.

days.title: Family tree
days.work: Draw a family tree with yourself, parents, and grandparents (and great-grandparents if known) with names and birthplaces.

days.title: Review
days.work: Start a family history book with the family tree and artifact pages.

weeks.assessment: Family tree and artifact pages.

objectives: Compare daily life with a parent or grandparent

days.title: Plan the interview
days.work: Write 6 interview questions for a grandparent or older relative (What toys did you play with? How did you get to school? What did you eat? What chores did you do?).

days.title: Interview
days.work: Conduct and record the interview by phone, video, or in person; take notes in drawings and words.

days.title: Compare
days.work: Make a Venn diagram comparing your daily life with the interviewee's childhood (school, games, technology, food).

days.title: Games from long ago
days.work: Play one game the interviewee played as a child (jacks, hopscotch, marbles) and write about it.

days.title: Review
days.work: Add the interview and Venn diagram to the family history book.

weeks.assessment: Interview notes and then/now Venn diagram.

weeks.topic: Family history book and unit check
objectives: Explain how sources tell us about the past
materials: LOC school photo from long ago

days.title: School long ago
days.work: Compare a Library of Congress photo of a one-room schoolhouse with your learning space today; list 4 differences.

days.title: Finish the book
days.work: Add a cover, a page 'How my life is different from my grandparent's,' and a page with a favorite family tradition.

days.title: Practice presenting
days.work: Practice telling your family story in 2 minutes using the book.

days.title: Present
days.work: Present the family history book to relatives (in person or by video).

days.title: Unit 1 check
days.work: Quiz: sort sources as primary/secondary, order events on a timeline, and name 2 ways life has changed.

weeks.assessment: Family history book presentation and unit quiz.

objectives: Identify title, legend, compass rose, scale, and date

days.title: What is a map
days.work: Compare a photo of a room taken from above with a map of the room; discuss what a bird's-eye view is.

days.title: Map elements
days.work: Find the title, legend (key), compass rose, scale, and date on three maps (zoo, park, city) and label them with sticky notes.

days.title: Directions
days.work: Use a real compass to find north in your home and label N, S, E, W on the walls; play a directions game ('take 3 steps north').

days.title: Map of my room
days.work: Draw a map of your bedroom with a title, key, and compass rose.

days.title: Review
days.work: Quiz: identify map elements on a new map and answer 4 direction questions.

weeks.assessment: Room map with all elements and map-elements quiz.

objectives: Locate places on a letter-number grid

days.title: Grid game
days.work: Play 'grid battleship' on a 5x5 letter-number grid to practice naming squares like C3.

days.title: Neighborhood map
days.work: Look at a printed map of your neighborhood with a grid overlay and find home, school, park, and store by grid square.

days.title: Relative location
days.work: Describe places using relative location ('The library is next to the park, north of my house').

days.title: Draw a grid map
days.work: Draw your own neighborhood map on grid paper with a key and list the grid square of 6 places.

days.title: Review
days.work: Answer 8 grid-location questions on a new community map.

weeks.assessment: Grid neighborhood map and location quiz.

objectives: Name the oceans around North America
Label a map of North America

days.title: Continents
days.work: Use a globe to find the 7 continents and 5 oceans; locate North America and the United States.

days.title: Countries
days.work: Label Canada, the United States, and Mexico on a blank map and color each; locate California.

days.title: Oceans
days.work: Label the Pacific, Atlantic, and Arctic Oceans and the Gulf of Mexico.

days.title: Map practice
days.work: Label the map from memory, check against an atlas, and fix mistakes.

days.title: Review
days.work: Map quiz: label 3 countries and 3 oceans from memory.

weeks.assessment: North America countries and oceans map quiz.

weeks.topic: North America: rivers, lakes, and mountains
objectives: Locate major rivers, the Great Lakes, and mountain ranges
Complete a North America map from memory

days.title: Mountains
days.work: Locate and label the Rocky Mountains, Appalachian Mountains, and Sierra Nevada on the map; build a clay model of the Rockies.

days.title: Rivers
days.work: Trace and label the Mississippi, Missouri, Colorado, and Rio Grande rivers; discuss why rivers matter to people.

days.title: Great Lakes
days.work: Learn the five Great Lakes with the mnemonic HOMES and label them.

days.title: Memory practice
days.work: Label the complete map from memory and check with an atlas.

days.title: Review
days.work: Map quiz: label countries, oceans, Great Lakes, 2 rivers, and 2 mountain ranges from memory.

weeks.assessment: Complete North America map from memory.

objectives: Tell when and how the family moved

days.title: Ask about moves
days.work: Interview a family member about where ancestors lived and when and why the family moved to your community.

days.title: Map the journey
days.work: Mark ancestors' homes on a world or U.S. map and connect them to your town with yarn or lines.

days.title: How they traveled
days.work: Learn how people traveled long ago (ship, wagon, train) and draw your family's journey.

days.title: Why people move
days.work: Discuss reasons people move (jobs, family, safety, land) and write one sentence about why your family moved.

days.title: Review
days.work: Add the map to the family history book and present it.

weeks.assessment: Family migration map and explanation.

objectives: Compare urban, suburban, and rural land use
materials: Calisphere photos of California cities, suburbs, and farms

days.title: Three communities
days.work: Look at photos of Los Angeles, a suburb, and a Central Valley farm and list what land is used for in each.

days.title: Compare
days.work: Make a three-column chart comparing housing, jobs, transportation, and land use.

days.title: Map it
days.work: Mark 3 urban, 3 suburban, and 3 rural places on a California map.

days.title: My community
days.work: Decide whether your community is urban, suburban, or rural and give 3 reasons.

days.title: Unit 2 check
days.work: Quiz on map elements, grids, North America labels, and land use types.

weeks.assessment: Land-use chart and unit quiz.

weeks.topic: Why we have rules and laws
objectives: Explain the purpose of rules and laws

days.title: Rules at home
days.work: List rules at home and explain why each one exists; discuss what would happen without them.

days.title: Laws in the community
days.work: Go on a walk to find signs (stop sign, speed limit, no littering) and write the law each shows.

days.title: Rule or law
days.work: Sort 10 examples into rules (home, school, game) and laws (community, state, country).

days.title: Fair rules
days.work: Make up a new game and write 3 fair rules; test whether they work.

days.title: Review
days.work: Explain in writing why laws keep people safe and treat people fairly.

weeks.assessment: Rule/law sort and written explanation.

objectives: Identify local, state, and national lawmakers
materials: photos of the U.S. Capitol and California State Capitol

days.title: Lawmakers
days.work: Learn that city councils, the California State Legislature in Sacramento, and Congress in Washington, D.C., make laws; look at photos of each building.

days.title: How a bill becomes a law
days.work: Follow a simple flow chart of how an idea becomes a law (idea → bill → vote → signed).

days.title: Family vote
days.work: Propose a 'family law' (e.g., a new pet rule), debate it, and vote on it.

days.title: Local leaders
days.work: Find the names of your mayor and governor and write one question you would ask them.

days.title: Review
days.work: Draw a flow chart of how a law is made.

weeks.assessment: Lawmaking flow chart.

objectives: Explain how laws are carried out
Explain how courts decide if laws were broken

days.title: Carrying out laws
days.work: Learn how mayors, governors, the president, and police carry out laws.

days.title: Courts
days.work: Learn how judges and juries decide whether a law was broken; look at a photo of a courtroom.

days.title: Mock trial
days.work: Role-play a mock trial of Goldilocks with judge, jury, and witnesses.

days.title: Consequences
days.work: Discuss fair consequences for breaking rules and laws.

days.title: Review
days.work: Match roles (lawmaker, judge, police officer, president) to their jobs.

weeks.assessment: Role-matching quiz and mock trial participation.

weeks.topic: Government in other countries and unit check
objectives: Compare how other countries make and carry out laws
materials: photos of Canada's Parliament and Mexico's Congress

days.title: Canada
days.work: Learn how Canada's Parliament makes laws and compare to Congress.

days.title: Mexico
days.work: Learn how Mexico's Congress and president work and compare to the U.S.

days.title: Compare
days.work: Make a chart comparing lawmakers and leaders in 3 countries.

days.title: Primary source
days.work: Look at the Preamble to the U.S. Constitution (National Archives) and discuss 'promote the general welfare.'

days.title: Unit 3 check
days.work: Quiz on making, carrying out, and judging laws.

weeks.assessment: Government comparison chart and unit quiz.

days.title: Label hunt
days.work: Look at labels on 10 household items to find where they were made; mark the countries on a world map.

days.title: Why trade
days.work: Learn that nations trade to get things they cannot make or grow; discuss bananas from Central America and almonds exported from California.

days.title: Trade game
days.work: Play a trading game where each player has different goods and must trade to make a complete set.

days.title: California exports
days.work: Read about California products sent around the world (almonds, movies, technology).

days.title: Review
days.work: Write 3 sentences about why trade helps nations.

weeks.assessment: Trade map and written explanation.

materials: LOC photo of 1912 cherry tree planting in Washington, D.C.

days.title: Cherry trees
days.work: Look at a Library of Congress photo of the 1912 planting of cherry trees given by Japan to Washington, D.C., and discuss why nations give gifts.

days.title: Peace Arch
days.work: Learn about the Peace Arch on the U.S.–Canada border and what it symbolizes.

days.title: Treaties
days.work: Learn that a treaty is an agreement between nations; make a class 'treaty' with a sibling about sharing toys.

days.title: Cultural exchange
days.work: Learn a song, food, or game from another country and share it.

days.title: Review
days.work: Explain one way nations share culture and one way they make agreements.

weeks.assessment: Primary source analysis and treaty.

days.title: Diplomacy
days.work: Learn that diplomats talk to solve problems between nations; role-play two 'countries' solving a water-sharing problem.

days.title: United Nations
days.work: Learn about the United Nations, founded in San Francisco in 1945; look at a photo of the signing.

days.title: Conflict resolution
days.work: Practice peaceful problem-solving steps with scenario cards.

days.title: When talking fails
days.work: Discuss briefly that sometimes nations use military force and why peace is preferred.

days.title: Unit 4 check
days.work: Quiz on trade, cultural contacts, treaties, and diplomacy.

weeks.assessment: Role-play and unit quiz.

objectives: Explain how producers and consumers depend on each other

days.title: Goods and services
days.work: Sort 12 picture cards into goods (bread, shoes) and services (haircut, doctor visit).

days.title: Producers
days.work: Interview a family member about their job: do they produce goods or provide services?

days.title: Consumers
days.work: List things your family bought this week and identify each as a good or service.

days.title: Interdependence
days.work: Draw a web showing how a baker depends on farmers, customers, and truck drivers.

days.title: Review
days.work: Write 3 sentences about how buyers and sellers need each other.

weeks.assessment: Goods/services sort and interdependence web.

objectives: Trace food from farm to table
Identify farmers, processors, distributors, and sellers

days.title: Milk's journey
days.work: Trace milk from cow to dairy to truck to store to your fridge and draw a flowchart.

days.title: Cereal journey
days.work: Trace a box of cereal from wheat field to factory to store.

days.title: Grocery visit
days.work: Visit a grocery store and find 5 foods grown in California.

days.title: Jobs
days.work: Match food jobs to their roles (farmer, processor, distributor, grocer).

days.title: Review
days.work: Explain the farm-to-table steps for one food.

weeks.assessment: Farm-to-table flowchart.

objectives: Compare food production long ago and today
materials: Calisphere photos of California farms in the early 1900s

days.title: Farms long ago
days.work: Look at Calisphere photos of early California farms and list tools and animals used.

days.title: Farms today
days.work: Compare with photos of modern farms (tractors, irrigation).

days.title: Food memories
days.work: Ask a grandparent how food was bought and cooked when they were young.

days.title: Preserving food
days.work: Learn how food was preserved long ago (canning, drying) and make dried apple slices with an adult.

days.title: Review
days.work: Venn diagram of food production long ago and today.

weeks.assessment: Long ago/today Venn diagram.

objectives: Identify land and water resources farms need

days.title: Weather and crops
days.work: Read short scenarios (a frost on orange trees, heavy rain at strawberry harvest, a heat wave) and tell how each changes how much food farmers can sell.

days.title: Water for farms
days.work: Look at photos of the California Aqueduct and Central Valley irrigation canals and trace on a map how Sierra snowmelt reaches farms.

days.title: Water test
days.work: Plant beans in two cups, giving one plenty of water and one very little, and record growth twice this week to see why farmers need water.

days.title: Drought choices
days.work: Read about a California drought and discuss why some farmers left fields empty or planted crops that need less water.

days.title: Review
days.work: Write 3 sentences explaining how weather, land, and water affect the food we can buy.

weeks.assessment: Written explanation linking weather, land, and water to food production.

objectives: Make choices when resources are limited
Identify the trade-off in a choice

days.title: Scarcity
days.work: Share 5 crackers among 7 people and discuss what to do when there is not enough; define scarcity in your own words.

days.title: Menu choices
days.work: With $10 of play money, order from a pretend menu and write what you chose and what you gave up (the trade-off).

days.title: Farmer's choice
days.work: Plan a 20-square grid-paper farm with limited land and water; decide how many squares of almonds, tomatoes, and lettuce to plant and explain why.

days.title: Family grocery list
days.work: Help plan a real grocery list within a budget, crossing out wants that do not fit.

days.title: Review
days.work: Write about one choice you made this week, what you gave up, and why.

weeks.assessment: Trade-off explanations and grid-farm plan.

objectives: Explain how money makes trade easier than barter

days.title: Barter
days.work: Try to trade toys or snacks with family members without money and record what problems happen (not everyone wants what you have).

days.title: Money makes it easier
days.work: Read about how people long ago traded with shells, salt, and coins, and explain how money solves the barter problems.

days.title: Market prep
days.work: Make 5 items to sell (bookmarks or drawings), decide prices, and make a sign for your market stall.

days.title: Market day
days.work: Run a family market: sell your goods as a producer, then buy from a sibling or parent as a consumer; record sales.

days.title: Review
days.work: Write 3 sentences: what you produced, what you consumed, and how buyers and sellers needed each other.

weeks.assessment: Market sales record and reflection.

objectives: Research one food's path from farm to table
Explain the roles of producers and consumers

days.title: Choose a food
days.work: Choose a favorite food (strawberries, tortillas, rice, oranges) and find where it is grown in California on a map.

days.title: Research
days.work: Use 2 sources to find out who grows, processes, transports, and sells it and what weather and water it needs.

days.title: Poster
days.work: Make a farm-to-table poster with 5 steps, a map, and labels for each worker's job.

days.title: Present
days.work: Present the poster to family, explaining one way the food is grown differently today than long ago.

days.title: Unit 5 check
days.work: Quiz: goods vs. services, producers vs. consumers, farm-to-table steps, and a scarcity choice question.

weeks.assessment: Farm-to-table poster and unit quiz.

weeks.topic: What makes a hero? Abraham Lincoln
objectives: Identify character traits of people who make a difference
materials: copy of Grace Bedell's 1860 letter and Lincoln's reply

days.title: What is a hero
days.work: List people you admire and the traits that make them heroes (courage, honesty, kindness, perseverance); make a 'hero traits' chart to use all unit.

days.title: Lincoln's life
days.work: Read a picture-book biography of Abraham Lincoln and put 5 events on a timeline (log cabin, self-taught reader, lawyer, president, ended slavery).

days.title: Grace Bedell's letter
days.work: Read the 1860 letter from 11-year-old Grace Bedell suggesting Lincoln grow a beard and Lincoln's reply; discuss what it shows about him.

days.title: Lincoln's legacy
days.work: Look at Lincoln on the penny and five-dollar bill and the Lincoln Memorial photo; discuss why we still honor him and which traits he showed.

days.title: Review
days.work: Write a letter to a leader, as Grace did, giving one idea and a reason.

weeks.assessment: Lincoln timeline and letter to a leader.

weeks.topic: Sitting Bull and George Washington Carver
objectives: Explain how Sitting Bull led and protected his people
Explain how George Washington Carver helped farmers
materials: LOC photographs of Sitting Bull and of Carver at Tuskegee Institute

days.title: Sitting Bull
days.work: Read a short biography of Sitting Bull, Lakota leader, and discuss how he worked to protect his people's land and way of life.

days.title: Photo study
days.work: Study a Library of Congress photograph of Sitting Bull and answer: What do you see? What do you wonder? What does it tell us about him?

days.title: George Washington Carver
days.work: Read a biography of George Washington Carver and learn how he taught Southern farmers to rotate crops with peanuts to restore the soil.

days.title: Peanut products
days.work: Look at a list of products Carver developed and taste peanuts and sweet potatoes (check allergies); look at the LOC photo of Carver in his lab.

days.title: Review
days.work: Complete a hero-traits chart for Sitting Bull and Carver with evidence from the texts.

weeks.assessment: Hero-traits chart with evidence for two people.

weeks.topic: Science heroes: Louis Pasteur and Marie Curie
objectives: Explain how Louis Pasteur's work keeps food safe
Explain Marie Curie's discoveries and perseverance
materials: photo of Marie Curie in her lab

days.title: Louis Pasteur
days.work: Read a short biography of Louis Pasteur and find the word 'pasteurized' on a milk or juice carton; explain how heating kills germs.

days.title: Germs experiment
days.work: With an adult, leave a slice of bread out and keep another sealed; observe mold over the week and connect to Pasteur's discoveries about germs.

days.title: Marie Curie
days.work: Read a biography of Marie Curie and learn how she became the first woman to win a Nobel Prize and the first person to win two.

days.title: Perseverance
days.work: Look at a photo of Marie Curie in her laboratory and discuss how she kept working when people said women could not be scientists.

days.title: Review
days.work: Write 2 sentences each on how Pasteur and Curie made a difference in people's lives today.

weeks.assessment: Written comparison of two scientists' contributions.

objectives: Describe Albert Einstein's curiosity and ideas
Compare two people who made a difference
materials: biographies of Einstein and Golda Meir

days.title: Albert Einstein
days.work: Read a picture-book biography of Albert Einstein (e.g., On a Beam of Light by Jennifer Berne) and list the questions he asked as a child.

days.title: Curiosity
days.work: Write 3 'I wonder' questions of your own about the world, as Einstein did, and choose one to investigate.

days.title: Golda Meir
days.work: Read about Golda Meir, who grew up in Milwaukee, taught school, and became prime minister of Israel; locate Ukraine, the U.S., and Israel on a map.

days.title: Compare
days.work: Make a Venn diagram comparing Einstein and Meir (both immigrants, different kinds of work).

days.title: Review
days.work: Add both to the hero timeline and explain which trait each showed most.

weeks.assessment: Venn diagram and hero timeline entries.

objectives: Explain how Jackie Robinson broke baseball's color barrier
Analyze Jackie Robinson's letter to President Eisenhower
materials: Jackie Robinson biography (e.g., Teammates by Peter Golenbock)
Jackie Robinson's 1958 letter to President Eisenhower (National Archives/DocsTeach)

days.title: Teammates
days.work: Read Teammates by Peter Golenbock and discuss how Jackie Robinson and Pee Wee Reese showed courage in 1947.

days.title: Unfair rules
days.work: Learn what segregation meant and why it was unfair; discuss how Robinson stayed calm and kept playing.

days.title: Primary source letter
days.work: Read parts of Jackie Robinson's 1958 letter to President Eisenhower (DocsTeach) and discuss what he asked the President to do.

days.title: Play ball
days.work: Play catch and learn that Jackie Robinson's number 42 is retired by every Major League team; design a 'Jackie Robinson Day' poster.

days.title: Review
days.work: Write how Jackie Robinson made a difference for others, using one detail from the letter.

weeks.assessment: Written response using evidence from the primary-source letter.

weeks.topic: Rosa Parks, Martin Luther King Jr., and Ruby Bridges
objectives: Explain how civil rights leaders worked for fairness
materials: Rosa Parks' arrest record/fingerprint card (National Archives)
The Story of Ruby Bridges (Robert Coles)

days.title: Rosa Parks
days.work: Read a short biography of Rosa Parks and look at her 1955 arrest record from the National Archives; discuss why breaking an unfair rule took courage.

days.title: Dr. King
days.work: Listen to an excerpt of Dr. King's 'I Have a Dream' speech and write your own dream for a fair world.

days.title: Ruby Bridges
days.work: Read The Story of Ruby Bridges and discuss how a 6-year-old helped integrate a New Orleans school in 1960.

days.title: Timeline
days.work: Place 1947 (Jackie Robinson), 1955 (bus boycott), 1960 (Ruby Bridges), and 1963 (March on Washington) on the hero timeline.

days.title: Review
days.work: Explain how each person used peaceful action to make a difference.

weeks.assessment: Civil rights timeline and written explanation.

objectives: Explain how Chavez and Huerta helped California farmworkers
Connect to food and farming unit
materials: Calisphere photos of the 1966 Delano-to-Sacramento march

days.title: Cesar Chavez
days.work: Read Harvesting Hope and discuss what farmworkers' lives were like and why Chavez organized them.

days.title: The march
days.work: Trace the 1966 march from Delano to Sacramento on a California map (about 300 miles) and look at Calisphere photos of the marchers.

days.title: Dolores Huerta
days.work: Read about Dolores Huerta and the motto 'Sí, se puede' (Yes, we can); discuss her role as a leader and teacher.

days.title: Connect to food
days.work: Connect Chavez and Huerta to the farm-to-table unit: who picks the grapes and lettuce we buy?

days.title: Review
days.work: Write a short paragraph on how Chavez and Huerta made a difference for workers.

weeks.assessment: Paragraph and map of the march.

weeks.topic: Sally Ride and Ellen Ochoa: reaching for the stars
objectives: Explain how Sally Ride and Ellen Ochoa made history in space
materials: NASA photos of Sally Ride on STS-7 (1983)
biographies of Sally Ride and Ellen Ochoa

days.title: Sally Ride
days.work: Read a biography of Sally Ride, the first American woman in space (1983), who grew up in Los Angeles, and study a NASA photo of her on the shuttle.

days.title: Ellen Ochoa
days.work: Read about Ellen Ochoa from La Mesa, California, the first Hispanic woman in space and later director of Johnson Space Center.

days.title: Paper rockets
days.work: Build and launch straw paper rockets and discuss how Ride and Ochoa used science and engineering.

days.title: Inspire others
days.work: Discuss how Sally Ride started programs to get girls interested in science; write one way you could inspire someone.

days.title: Review
days.work: Add both astronauts to the hero timeline and chart their traits.

weeks.assessment: Hero-traits chart and timeline entries.

objectives: Identify people who make a difference locally
Recognize that ordinary people can be heroes

days.title: Local heroes
days.work: Brainstorm people who make a difference in your community (firefighters, librarians, volunteers, coaches, a family member).

days.title: Interview
days.work: Interview a community helper or volunteer in person or by phone using 5 prepared questions about why they do their work.

days.title: Fred Korematsu
days.work: Read about Fred Korematsu of Oakland, honored on California's Fred Korematsu Day (Jan. 30), who stood up for fairness for Japanese Americans.

days.title: Be a hero
days.work: Plan and do one helpful act for your community (pick up litter, donate books, make cards for a senior center).

days.title: Review
days.work: Write a thank-you card to your interviewee naming the trait you admire.

weeks.assessment: Interview notes, service act, and thank-you card.

objectives: Research one person who made a difference
Present as the hero in a living museum

days.title: Choose and research
days.work: Choose one hero from the unit (or another approved hero) and gather 6 facts from 2 sources: early life, challenge, action, and legacy.

days.title: Timeline and traits
days.work: Make a 5-event timeline and a list of 3 character traits with evidence for your hero.

days.title: Poster
days.work: Create a biography poster with a portrait, timeline, traits, and one primary source image or quote.

days.title: Rehearse
days.work: Write and practice a 1-minute speech in first person ('I am Sally Ride…').

days.title: Living museum
days.work: Present the living museum in costume to family and answer audience questions.

weeks.assessment: Biography poster and living-museum presentation (rubric).

objectives: Review family history, maps, government, economics, and heroes
Reflect on how people make a difference

days.title: Family history review
days.work: Reread the family history book and add one new page about this year's events.

days.title: Map from memory
days.work: Label a blank map of North America from memory (countries, oceans, Great Lakes, rivers, mountains) and compare with the fall map.

days.title: Government and economics
days.work: Play a review game matching vocabulary (law, judge, producer, consumer, trade, treaty) to meanings.

days.title: Heroes reflection
days.work: Write which hero inspired you most and how you could make a difference.

days.title: Year-end check
days.work: Take a year-end review quiz and share your favorite project from the year.

weeks.assessment: Map from memory and year-end quiz.

courses.subject: VAPA
courses.title: Art & Music 2
courses.description: A second-grade arts course that alternates visual art and music units, with a short dance and drama unit, aligned to the 2019 California Arts Standards. Students explore line, shape, color, texture, and form through drawing, painting, collage, clay, printmaking, and recycled sculpture while studying artists such as Kandinsky, Matisse, Van Gogh, Monet, and Louise Nevelson and art traditions from around the world. In music they keep a steady beat, read and write rhythms (ta, ti-ti, rest), sing sol-mi-la melodies, identify instrument families in Peter and the Wolf and Carnival of the Animals, and compose short pieces. The year ends with a home art exhibit and music performance.
courses.framework: 2019 California Arts Standards for Public Schools (Visual Arts, Music, Dance, Theatre); 2020 California Arts Education Framework
